subject: Computer Science
unit: AQA GCSE 8525 / Cambridge IGCSE 0478: Number systems
topic: Binary representations, hexadecimal and fixed-width arithmetic
scope: Both qualifications are untiered. The common work uses eight-bit positive values; sixteen-bit conversion, overflow and two’s complement are explicitly labelled IGCSE work here, not asserted to be requirements of AQA GCSE 8525. Original teaching and practice, not official examination material. Practice rubrics are for self-review. This topic does not establish whole-course coverage, independent subject review or publication approval.
prerequisites: Use powers of two and integer division.
Distinguish a value from the symbols used to represent it.
objectives: Convert values without changing their meaning.
Trace binary addition and logical shifts.
Distinguish unsigned and signed interpretations of the same bits.

notes.heading: Place value: GCSE/IGCSE untiered
paragraphs: An eight-bit unsigned pattern has weights 128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2 and 1 from left to right. Add the weights whose bits are 1. To encode 75, select 64, 8, 2 and 1, producing 01001011. The leading zero preserves the chosen width without changing the value. Eight bits give 256 distinct patterns, covering integers 0 through 255 when interpreted as unsigned; 256 is the count of patterns, not the largest value.

notes.heading: Hexadecimal and arithmetic: GCSE/IGCSE untiered
paragraphs: Hexadecimal uses sixteen digits, with A through F representing ten through fifteen. One hexadecimal digit corresponds to four bits, so 0100 1011 becomes 4B. Hexadecimal is a compact human-readable notation for the same bits; converting to it does not compress the underlying data. In binary addition, 1 + 1 writes 0 and carries 1, while 1 + 1 + 1 writes 1 and carries 1. Work from the least significant column and track each carry.

notes.heading: Logical shifts: GCSE/IGCSE untiered
paragraphs: A logical shift moves bits and inserts zeros. With sufficient width, shifting an unsigned integer left once multiplies it by two. In a fixed-width register, bits leaving an end are discarded, so that shortcut needs a condition. A right shift once divides an unsigned value by two and discards any fractional remainder. For 00001101, a right shift gives 00000110: 13 becomes 6, not 6.5. State both the pattern and its interpretation to show what was lost.

notes.heading: Signed values and wider conversion: IGCSE untiered
paragraphs: Cambridge 0478 includes conversions up to sixteen bits and eight-bit two’s complement. In eight-bit two’s complement the leftmost weight is -128, followed by the ordinary positive weights 64 down to 1. Thus 11111011 represents -128 + 64 + 32 + 16 + 8 + 2 + 1 = -5, although the same bits represent 251 if unsigned. To encode a negative value, invert the bits of its positive eight-bit representation and add one. The signed range is -128 to 127. An unsigned sum greater than 255 overflows eight bits; truncating a carry does not make the mathematical result correct.

steps: Group 1010 and 0110 to obtain A and 6.

workedExamples.prompt: IGCSE: encode -12 in eight-bit two’s complement.
steps: Write +12 as 00001100, invert to 11110011 and add one.

misconceptions.claim: Hexadecimal stores fewer underlying bits than the same binary value.
misconceptions.correction: It abbreviates how humans write a bit pattern; the representation choice alone does not compress data.

misconceptions.claim: A binary pattern has one meaning regardless of context.
misconceptions.correction: Encoding and signedness determine its interpretation.

questions.prompt: [GCSE/IGCSE: untiered] Convert 01011010 to denary and hexadecimal.
[GCSE/IGCSE: untiered] Encode denary 109 as eight-bit binary.
solution: Place ones at those weights and preserve eight positions.

questions.prompt: [GCSE/IGCSE: untiered] Add 00101101 and 00010111, showing the eight-bit result.
[GCSE/IGCSE: untiered] Logically shift 00010111 right by one position and explain the denary result.
solution: The least significant 1 is lost and zero enters at the left.

questions.prompt: [IGCSE: untiered] Add unsigned denary 200 and 100 in an eight-bit register. Explain why storing only the low eight bits is wrong.
questions.answer: The true sum is 300; the retained value is 44 because the 256 carry is lost.
solution: Eight bits represent at most 255 unsigned.

questions.prompt: [IGCSE: untiered] Interpret 11110110 as eight-bit two’s complement, then encode hexadecimal 12AF as sixteen-bit binary.

revisionGuide.summary: Keep the value, encoding and register width distinct. Board-specific material is explicitly labelled rather than invented as a higher tier.
keyIdeas: What is the maximum eight-bit unsigned integer? 255.
How many bits match one hexadecimal digit? Four.
What is hexadecimal F? Denary 15, binary 1111.
What happens to the remainder in an unsigned right shift? It is discarded.
What is the eight-bit two’s-complement range? -128 to 127; labelled IGCSE content here.
